content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary

In this episode I will identify the essential, standards-based skills that we are to teach within narrative writing units.

Narrative writing includes many different genres. For example:
--A Personal Narrative is a true story about one's own experience.
--Realistic Fiction is a made-up story that COULD happen in real life.
--Fantasies involve magical or supernatural elements.
--Plays or Dramas are stories written in script form and told through performance.
--And Graphic Novels tell stories through a mix of visual art and text.

More unique narrative genres include stories written in response to a text read. For example:
--After reading literature, Continue the Story by imagining what happens next or exploring a future event.
--After reading a story, you can Retell it from another Character's Perspective.
--You can write Fiction Based on Fact. Create a fictional story inspired by information learned from nonfiction texts.

section_name: Narrative Writing Standards and the 4 Essential Skills
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Standards and the 4 Essential Skills

Now your state standards likely don't name the specific types or genres you are to tackle. Rather they more broadly state that you are to teach students how to compose or write narratives.

Let's look at a couple grade-level standards for instructional expectations:

--Kindergarten, in most states, reads something like this: "Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to narrate a single event or several loosely linked events. Tell about the events in the order in which they occurred, and provide a reaction to what happened."

--Let's jump up and look at a second grade writing standard. "Write narratives of a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events. Include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings. Use transitions to signal event order and provide a sense of closure."

--All grade levels are building on one another. And by fourth grade, the expectations include: "Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events. Establish a situation and introduce a narrator and/or characters. Organize an event sequence using a variety of transitional words and phrases. Develop experiences with dialogue, description, and sensory details. Provide a conclusion that follows from the narrated experiences or events."

For most teachers, the skills outlined in the standards are likely not surprising. However, simply listing character actions, thoughts and feelings does not qualify as a narrative according to the standards. SomeTHING must happen to someONE. This is what is meant by an "event" or "experience"--there is a conflict or problem that eventually gets solved or resolved.

Consequently, looking across the elementary expectations, there are clearly 4 skills that we must include within our narrative writing instruction. How to:
1. Describe a problem
2. Conclude with a solution
3. Reveal the character this happens to
4. Sequence the details

Throughout this episode, we will look closely at these 4 essential ingredients of narrative writing. Specifically, what each skill looks like across the grade levels and the key points to make within your Tier 1 whole-class mini-lessons.

Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #1: Describe a Problem

It is a common misconception that narrative writing is the easiest of the three writing modes. In reality, conveying information and sharing an opinion tend to come more naturally to students. Narrative writing requires more than just telling the reader something--he has to take him on a ride through the story arc. And this does not come naturally to students. Rather, they introduce characters and describe in great detail where they go, what they do, who they see and what they say... until they finally just go to bed.

Let me show you what I mean. A kindergartener wrote: "Once me and my dad took a walk to the park. And then we sat on the soccer field to relax. Then we saw a falcon soaring in the air. 'Look,' I said. 'It's beautiful.' My dad said, 'I agree.'"

Although any kindergarten teacher would be over the moon with this writing--as it's fabulous and long!--it lacks any type of problem. It's much more of an informative piece where the young writer is telling the reader about something.

Without instruction on the importance of a problem, students continue to just tell character details as they move up the grade levels. Here's a great piece of second-grade writing, but again, it's not a narrative: "Me and my dad played in the snow. We made a snowman. My dad pulled me on the sled. It was fun. We had a snowball fight. My dad buried me in the snow. We made a snowman family--a mom, dad, and a kid. We made them a house. I made the roof. My dad made the door. We had so much fun. I went inside to play and drink hot chocolate."

Again--yes, it's great writing, but there is no problem. And if we don't teach that key facet of narrative writing, then they just write longer and longer character descriptions with a lot of and-then, and-then, and-then.

section_name: Skill #1: Fifth Grade Example and Airplane Analogy
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #1: Fifth Grade Example and Airplane Analogy

Here's a fifth grade example:

"Girls Day Out! My sister Sabrina, my mom, and I went to the Columbian Park Zoo and looked at all of the different kinds of animals. Some of them were very unusual. Then we went to the park and played for a while. After we went to the park, we decided to get something to eat. Since it was so hot, we went to the Lafayette Waterpark, and we went on slides and played in the pool. We went on the lazy river and went out the shoot-out slides. We walked across the 'gator walk.' We got a snack at the food area, and when it was time to go, right outside of the waterpark were rides. We went on a few of them. It was a lot of fun. Then we went to Walmart and got some clothes and looked around for a while. Then we were on our way back home and the day had flown by. So when we got home, my sister and I played outside and that was it--the day was over, but it sure was a great day."

See what I mean. It's a list of things the characters did and settings they went to, but it's not really a story. Now, imagine teaching these 3 kids how to write a narrative that actually includes a problem!

Think of narrative writing like an airplane flight. The Problem is what propels the story forward, just like takeoff drives the excitement of a flight. But without a problem, the plane never lifts off. It's as if the writer drove the plane from point A to point B. Sitting on the tarmac IS part of the journey--but the excitement begins when the plane lifts off!

Similarly, character and setting ARE necessary for a story--but they're NOT the key ingredients. The character is NOT the main idea--the problem he faces is.

section_name: Skill #1: Three Types of Character Problems
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #1: Three Types of Character Problems

In truth, a strong story can start with little more than a character's name and vague location. Check out the first lines of these picture books:
--"My dad and I live in an airport."
--"Lilly loved school."
--"My name is Humpty Dumpty, and this was my favorite spot, high up on the wall."
--"In the light of the moon, a little egg lay on a leaf."

Rather than starting narrative instruction focused on characterization, begin with the most important part--the problem.

Teach students that there are three broad categories or types of character problems. The main character can have a problem with: someONE, someTHING, or himSELF. We can help students remember their 3 options by pairing each one with an emoji.

--In stories where the main character has a problem with someone, then the middle describes WHO he is upset with and WHY. (e.g., an individual, a group/society).

--In narratives where the main character has a problem with something, this includes describing something physical that is lost, missing, broken or not working, or any situation that is really no one's fault. (e.g., unavoidable situation, an accident, the weather/nature, failed technology).

--And in stories where the main character has a problem with himself, then the middle is about a fear the character has to overcome, or a tough choice he has to make, or a behavior he needs to change. (e.g., his feelings, his attitude).

section_name: Skill #1: Teaching Students to Plan Story Problems
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #1: Teaching Students to Plan Story Problems

Use this information to model how writers come up with story problems using photographs. Reveal a scene that your students can relate to. Point out the character and setting that are obvious in the picture. Remind students that every story has something happen that is bad, wrong, or dangerous, and yet the characters in this picture are not hurt, not upset, nothing is wrong... yet.

Model how to think about what COULD happen? What could go wrong? Brainstorm multiple possibilities that are realistic for the characters and setting in the photograph. For example, these two boys are building a sandcastle at the beach and:
--One character accidentally flicks sand in the eye of the other. (problem with someONE)
--The tide comes in and washes away their sand castle. (problem with someTHING)
--They find a diamond ring buried in the sand and want to keep it for themselves. (problem with himSELF)

When first teaching students how to plan a story's problem, model the process several times using different photos. After modeling several different problem possibilities, then teach students how to narrow down to one. It may be the one they know the most about, and/or is the most realistic for the situation, and/or is the most interesting. Emphasize the importance of choosing and writing about one problem that the character faces. Remember, this is the main idea--so the story needs to be focused around a single problem.

After plenty of instruction and practice with photographs, transition to personal narrative topics. Guide students to brainstorm times in their own lives when they were mad, sad or hurt. Have them list multiple times they had a problem with someONE, with someTHING, and even with themSELVES. Have them write out the problem in just a couple sentences. And knowing it's part of the story's middle, have them place it lower on the paper. Provide students lots of practice with this skill by having them write out the general problem for all of the topics they came up with. Expect this from young writers, too--even if they aren't yet writing sentences. Model the same process by drawing and labeling each problem on its own sheet of paper. For example this first grader wrote: "My hamster bit me on the fenger."

After explicit instruction and plenty of guided practice in planning story problems, then transition to teaching students how to integrate a solution--and that's essential skill #2.

Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #2: Conclude with a Solution

Writers must plan the ending, and that means planning how the problem gets solved. The character's problem can't just keep going on and on, just like an airplane can't keep going up and up. It has to eventually land--and the landing of a story is the solution.

However, simply ending with "The end" or "I went to bed" or "I woke up and it was all a dream" does not actually fix the problem. Remind students that they are writing for an audience who wants to know how it turns out--they need the end to include a solution.

In order to do this, teach students 3 types of solutions that they can use in their own narratives. And again, tie them to emojis.

--Someone helps fix the problem. Like another character can pitch in, have an idea, or apologize to make things better.

--Or, the main character tries different things until someTHING finally works and fixes the problem.

--Or, the problem improves and the character starts to feel better after time passes and his attitude or feelings change.

Teach students ways to solve their characters' problems--they need to know their options.

After this instruction, model how to think of possible story solutions to the problems generated from the original photographs. Again, model how to choose the best option--the most realistic and interesting solution. Continue refining students' understanding of how to "land" a story by having them return to their own narrative quickwrites and insert a solution near the bottom of the paper. Task them only to write a 1-or-2-sentence solution, but to do this for several different problems they've started.

Because younger students tend to write so big, consider taping a new sheet of paper to the right of each problem. This further demonstrates that the solution comes after the problem. Back to the first grader whose hamster bit his finger. The solution was: "Then my mom put a bandade on my fanger. Yay!"

Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #3: Reveal the Character

So far, we've learned that the main idea of a narrative is its plot--a problem that gets solved. Now that the main idea is covered, we pivot our instruction to how a story starts--with the revealing of character and setting. (Essential skill #3.)

If we consider that the problem is what happens in the story, and the solution is how it gets fixed, we now need to focus on who the problem happens to and where it all takes place.

The "problem" belongs to someone and that character needs to be identified quickly. In personal narratives, this is the writer himself, usually resulting in the use of first-person pronouns--"I," "me," and "my." However, in most other narrative genres, the reader needs to know a little more about the character.

In addition to identifying the character, the beginning of the story also includes the most important details about the setting--but only the most important ones. In fact, if we revisit the standards from earlier, most grade-level expectations don't require setting details at all! The highlighted text shows we need to teach characters, problems, and solutions. But if we look at the unhighlighted text, there's no mention of setting! This reinforces why students should not write long, drawn-out openings that delay the problem. Remember the airplane analogy: We don't want to stay on the tarmac; we want to lift off!

That all said, I think it is important to provide the reader a little context for where the character is when this problem occurs. The reader needs to see the character in a scene before the problem arises. He should be shown in a neutral or positive light--happy, content, and experiencing things going well--so that when the problem occurs, it creates a clear contrast and makes it feel more significant.

section_name: Skill #3: Choosing Important Character and Setting Details
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #3: Choosing Important Character and Setting Details

Return to the photo examples used to generate problems and solutions. Review the basic character and setting information that originally inspired the problem. What did you say about the photo regarding who and where? Probably something like: "2 boys are building a sand castle at the beach." There, that's it. That's all you needed to come up with a problem, so that's likely all the reader needs, as well. Model how to stretch that into 1-2 sentences. "Two boys were at the beach... playing in the sand."

I know you could add much more about the characters--like how old they are, the color of their swimsuits, if they're friends or brothers. You could also say it's a nice sunny day, give the temperature, and name the beach they are at. But all of this isn't necessary for the problem to occur.

--Sand is at a beach--that's a setting detail the reader needs. But the fact that it's 80 degrees or 95 degrees doesn't make a difference to this problem.

--An important character detail is that the boys are building a sand castle--but their ages or the colors of their swimsuits are not.

While teaching students all the many character and setting details they could include, emphasize how to decide the important from unimportant ones. Remind them that the story "gets good" when the problem is revealed--so we don't want to postpone it too long. While the airplane doesn't go from the tarmac to 30,000 feet immediately--it only needs a little runway. Stories only need a little background information upfront.

After practicing the choosing of important character and setting details for the photographs, students can return to their previous personal narratives for further experience.
--Intermediate students can add 1-2 sentences at the top of the paper.
--And primary students can tape on a piece of paper to the left of each problem!

The hamster-bite story actually began like this: "One time when my cousins were at my house..."

Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Skill #4: Sequence the Details

At this point, all grade levels understand that narratives have three parts: characters in a setting, who face a problem, that gets solved. While this may be the full focus in K-1, grades 2 and up have to write longer sequenced stories. This is essential skill #4.

The key to writing a longer story is not adding more after the end, but stretching the middle. Move the problem to the far right of the organizer, leaving space for more middle details. Remind students that the problem is in the middle--but it's the beginning of the middle. They can make their stories longer by adding details between the problem and its solution.

Writers describe the character's thoughts, feelings, reactions, and dialogue during the problem. Returning to the quickwrite about the boys finding the diamond ring, this might include description of their excitement and first thoughts about becoming rich. But then there could be dialogue between them, where one boy is starting to feel guilty and wants to turn the ring in.

Encourage students to think of this as writing in slow-motion, adding details one by one, in order and in sequence. This is how they achieve a "well-elaborated event" or "developed experience."

For any intermediate teacher questioning minimizing character details at the beginning of a narrative, this is where they should live--after the problem is revealed. These details will be much more interesting and relevant!

And although the standards may not up the ante on K-1 writers, they are definitely able to achieve this skill. In fact, the first grader who wrote about his hamster bite actually included 2 more sentences after the problem. After the hamster bit his finger, he wrote "Ouch!" to represent a feeling and perhaps even early dialogue. And to describe the injury itself, he added: "It was bleding and stinging rily bad."

By teaching students how to stretch the middle, we maintain the integrity of the story arc, while developing longer, stronger narratives.

Episode 8 | Narrative for Elementary — Closing Takeaways

As I wrap up this video, let me identify 2 important takeaways.

First, teaching students to write narratives means teaching them to plan problems in their stories. Without an "uh-oh" or "oh-no" event, it's just a list of what someone did.

And second, be mindful of what you call a story from now on. Once students understand narratives are about characters who solve problems, then it will be confusing for you to tell them to "write a story" during a persuasive or informative writing unit.

That said, I encourage you to apply these four essential skills when teaching students about narrative writing, and by doing this, we take the next step toward building better writers.
